Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Voters in Nashville, Tennessee -- a city that has seen a dramatic increase in its immigrant population -- rejected a measure Thursday that would have made English the only language used for government business in its metropolitan area. Nearly 57 percent of those who cast ballots Thursday in Nashville, Tennessee, voted against the measure. With all 173 precincts reporting, 41,752 voters, or nearly 57 percent, voted against the proposed amendment, with 32,144 voters supporting it, according to unofficial results posted on the Nashville city government Web site. "No person shall have a right to government services in any other language," the proposal read. The measure would have included government meetings. The Metropolitan Council, which submitted the measure, could have mandated exceptions to protect public health and safety. Elise Shore, southeast director of the Mexican-American Legal Defense and Educational Fund, said her regional office in Atlanta, Georgia, was monitoring the Nashville balloting. "We just elected our first black president. There are the forces of globalization and conducting business around the world ... in the face of this, we see these measures?" Shore asked. The proposal "sends a strong message ... this is a negative message. In fact, it invites discrimination," she said. In a newspaper editorial published Thursday, The Tennessean urged voters to defeat the proposal. "This amendment would exclude and marginalize those residents and visitors to Nashville simply because English is not their native tongue," the editorial said. The polls opened at 7 a.m. and closed at 7 p.m. Before the measure was defeated, a spokesman for U.S. English Inc., an action group that supports English-only laws nationwide, said the Nashville proposal was a good one. "Government programs are aimed at helping people reach self-sufficiency and success," Rob Toonkel said. "Allowing use of a second language doesn't encourage them to learn English." "The key word [of the amendment] is 'actions that bind the government,' " Toonkel said, which would cover transactions such as getting a city contract. If a non-English speaker needs help filling out a form, and someone in that agency speaks their language, they should be helped, he said. "But you shouldn't be able to come in, pick up a form [in another language] and leave." According to Toonkel, about 30 states and more than 100 localities have made English their official language, and he said his organization believes such laws are legal. Raul Gonzalez, legislative director for the National Council of La Raza, said the message of the proposal is discriminatory. "What it ... says is, 'If you speak a language other than English, you may not be welcome here,' " Gonzalez said. La Raza is a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization focused on reducing poverty and discrimination and improving opportunities for Hispanic Americans. Gonzalez said similar English-only laws across the country "have so many exceptions they are meaningless." In an editorial earlier this month, The Tennessean quoted the referendum's sponsor, Councilman Eric Crafton, who said the bill was needed to save the city $100,000 to $150,000 in annual translation and related costs. However, metro officials told the newspaper such services are provided by employees already on the city's payroll. The council passed a similar bill in 2007, but it was vetoed by then-Mayor Bill Purcell, who called it "unconstitutional, unnecessary and mean-spirited," according to The Tennessean. U.S. Census data from 2000 showed an increase of 210 percent in the immigrant population of the Nashville metro area, including Davidson County, since 1990. During that decade, immigrants accounted for 45 percent of the overall population increase in the city. More than two-thirds, or 67 percent, of the area's foreign-born population had entered since 1990. This was much higher than the rate for the state overall, which was about 58 percent. The Census Bureau's American Community Survey, taken between 2005 and 2007 for the Nashville metro area, shows a population of 613,632. Of that number, 61,843 were foreign-born, with most of the immigrants coming from Latin America. About 73,000 residents speak a language other than English at home and, of those, 35,290 speak English less than "very well," the survey found.

# Nashville Voters Reject English-Only Ballot Measure

Nashville, Tennessee, became the center of a heated national debate over language rights and immigration policy when voters went to the polls to decide on a ballot measure that would have mandated English as the sole language for nearly all government business and services within the city. The proposal, which emerged against the backdrop of the city's rapidly diversifying population, sought to prohibit Metro Nashville government agencies from communicating with the public in any language other than English, with only narrow exceptions for matters involving public health, safety, and constitutionally protected rights.

## Background and Context

The measure arrived at a moment when Nashville was experiencing significant demographic change. Over the preceding decade, the city had seen substantial growth in its immigrant and refugee communities, drawn by employment opportunities, resettlement programs, and the broader economic expansion of the metropolitan area. This influx transformed neighborhoods across the city and brought a new mix of languages into schools, workplaces, and public offices, prompting both celebration of Nashville's growing diversity and anxiety among some residents about cultural and linguistic change.

Supporters of the ballot measure argued that requiring government to operate exclusively in English would unify the city around a common language, reduce translation costs for taxpayers, and—perhaps most centrally to their argument—compel new immigrants to learn English more quickly. They contended that providing government services in multiple languages inadvertently allowed immigrants to avoid learning English, thereby delaying their integration into American economic and civic life. In their view, mandating English-only communication was less about exclusion and more about promoting self-sufficiency, arguing that fluency in English was the surest path to opportunity and independence for newcomers.

## The Debate

The measure drew attention and involvement from national organizations with long histories on opposite sides of the language rights debate. U.S. English Inc., an organization that has advocated for English as the official language of government at various levels across the country, supported the Nashville proposal, framing it as a common-sense measure to preserve linguistic unity and streamline government operations.

On the other side, the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF) and other civil rights organizations mobilized against the measure, warning that it would have far-reaching discriminatory consequences. Critics argued that the proposal would effectively cut off non-English-speaking residents—including legal immigrants, refugees, and long-time citizens with limited English proficiency—from essential city services, emergency communications, and civic participation. They characterized the measure as part of a broader pattern of English-only initiatives nationwide that, despite being framed in unifying language, functioned to marginalize immigrant communities and signal hostility toward the city's newest residents. Opponents also raised concerns about the practical and economic fallout, suggesting that the measure could damage Nashville's reputation as a welcoming, business-friendly city and complicate efforts by police, fire, and health departments to serve all residents effectively.

The campaign became a flashpoint that drew coverage well beyond Tennessee, as advocates and opponents alike recognized it as a test case for how mid-sized American cities undergoing rapid demographic transformation would navigate questions of language, identity, and inclusion.

## The Outcome

When the votes were tallied, Nashville residents rejected the measure decisively, with nearly 57 percent voting against the amendment. The defeat was widely interpreted as a significant statement from the city's electorate, signaling that a majority of voters were unwilling to embrace a policy that critics had labeled discriminatory and exclusionary.

For opponents of the measure, the result was celebrated as a victory that averted what they viewed as a harmful and divisive policy—one that could have alienated immigrant communities, hampered access to city services, and tarnished Nashville's image as a growing, cosmopolitan city. Civil rights advocates framed the outcome as evidence that voters, even amid ongoing national debates over immigration, were willing to reject measures perceived as punitive toward newcomers.

Proponents of the measure, while disappointed, maintained that their underlying goals—encouraging English acquisition and fostering immigrant self-sufficiency—remained worthwhile objectives, even if this particular legislative approach had failed to win public support. The debate in Nashville ultimately became a notable example in the broader national conversation about language policy, immigration, and the balance between civic unity and inclusivity in American cities.

# Nashville Voters Reject English-Only Measure in Blow to National Movement

Nashville voters delivered a decisive rejection of a controversial ballot measure that would have mandated English as the sole language for government business, dealing a setback to English-only advocates who had hoped the Music City vote would provide momentum for similar efforts nationwide.

The amendment, which would have required nearly all official city communications to be conducted exclusively in English, failed by a significant margin, with opponents arguing it would have created barriers to essential services for the city's growing immigrant population.

## The Metropolitan Council's Role

The measure's journey to the ballot began after it failed to gain traction through conventional legislative channels. Unable to secure passage through the Metropolitan Council, Nashville's governing legislative body, proponents gathered petition signatures to force a public referendum—a move that supporters characterized as pure democracy in action, while critics called it an end-run around elected officials who had already signaled the measure's problems.

Metropolitan Council members who had opposed the measure during earlier deliberations pointed to practical concerns: emergency services, public health communications, and basic government functions could all be compromised if translators and multilingual materials were suddenly prohibited. Council opponents also raised concerns about potential legal challenges and the financial cost of defending the amendment against constitutional questions.

## National Organizations Weigh In

The Nashville vote attracted attention far beyond city limits, becoming a proxy battle for national organizations with starkly different visions of American linguistic identity.

U.S. English Inc., the Washington-based advocacy group that has pushed English-only legislation in states and municipalities across the country for decades, backed the Nashville measure as consistent with its mission. The organization has long argued that a common language serves as a unifying force for civic participation and that government operations should default to English to encourage assimilation and reduce translation costs.

Standing in opposition, the National Council of La Raza (NCLR), one of the nation's most prominent Hispanic advocacy organizations, campaigned against the measure, framing it as part of a troubling pattern of legislation that could marginalize Spanish-speaking residents and other non-English speakers. NCLR representatives argued that such measures often function less as practical governance tools and more as symbolic statements that alienate immigrant communities, potentially discouraging civic engagement rather than encouraging it.

## A Changing City Weighs In

Nashville's rejection of the amendment reflects the city's rapid demographic transformation. Once considered a relatively homogeneous Southern capital, Nashville has seen substantial growth in its immigrant and refugee populations over the past two decades, with communities from Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia reshaping neighborhoods across Davidson County.

Business leaders had also voiced opposition to the measure, with some citing concerns that an English-only mandate could tarnish the city's reputation as a welcoming destination for tourism, corporate relocation, and international investment—all critical components of Nashville's economic growth strategy.

## Broader Implications

The defeat represents a significant setback for U.S. English Inc. and allied organizations that have found more success in other states, where more than thirty have adopted some form of official English legislation. Nashville's rejection suggests that urban centers experiencing rapid diversification may prove more resistant to such measures than state legislatures, where rural and suburban voting blocs often hold greater sway.

For the National Council of La Raza, the outcome offers validation of grassroots organizing strategies employed against similar measures nationally, reinforcing the argument that direct community engagement can overcome well-funded advocacy campaigns.

As cities across the country continue to grapple with questions of language policy and civic inclusion, Nashville's vote will likely be studied by both sides as either a cautionary tale or a roadmap—depending on which side of the debate is doing the analysis.

# Nashville Voters Reject English-Only Measure Again, Reflecting City's Changing Demographics

NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Nashville voters have once again rejected a proposal to make English the city's official language, marking the second time in recent history that such a measure has failed despite support from some local officials and advocacy groups.

The measure, which would have required most government business to be conducted exclusively in English, failed by a significant margin in Tuesday's election, according to results from the Davidson County Election Commission. The outcome echoes a similar rejection of English-only legislation in 2007, when then-Mayor Karl Dean vetoed a comparable ordinance passed by the Metro Council, calling it harmful to the city's economic development and international reputation.

"This is not new territory for Nashville," said Maria Gonzalez, a longtime community organizer with the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition. "In 2007, we saw the city reject this kind of exclusionary policy, and voters have essentially reaffirmed that decision today."

## Historical Context

The 2007 measure, championed by then-Councilman Eric Crafton, would have mandated that all official city communications be conducted solely in English, with limited exceptions for public health and safety matters. Mayor Dean's veto at the time drew national attention, with business leaders warning that the ordinance could deter international investment and tourism in a city increasingly marketing itself as "Music City" to a global audience.

A subsequent referendum in January 2009 saw voters reject the English-only proposal by a roughly 57% to 43% margin, effectively ending Crafton's yearslong push for the policy.

## Demographic Shifts

Nashville's immigrant population has grown substantially since that 2009 vote. According to data from the Migration Policy Institute and U.S. Census Bureau, the foreign-born population in the Nashville metropolitan area has nearly doubled over the past 15 years, now representing more than 12% of the region's residents.

The city has seen particularly significant growth in its Kurdish, Hispanic, and Southeast Asian communities. Nashville is home to the largest Kurdish population in the United States, concentrated in the area often referred to as "Little Kurdistan" in South Nashville. Hispanic residents now make up roughly 10% of Davidson County's population, up from about 4.6% in 2000.

"The Nashville of today looks very different from the Nashville of 2007," said Vanderbilt University sociologist Dr. James Chen, who studies immigration patterns in the Southeast. "These demographic changes have real political consequences. Immigrant communities have become more organized, more civically engaged, and more integrated into the city's economic and cultural fabric."

## Business Community Response

As in 2007, Nashville's business community largely opposed the English-only measure. The Nashville Area Chamber of Commerce issued a statement prior to the vote expressing concern that the ordinance could undermine the city's efforts to attract international business and talent.

"Nashville has positioned itself as a global city," the Chamber's statement read. "Measures that signal exclusion rather than welcome run counter to our economic interests."

## Looking Forward

Supporters of the failed measure expressed disappointment but vowed to continue pushing for similar legislation in the future.

"We believe English should be our common language for government functions," said local activist Robert Hastings, who helped organize support for the measure. "This isn't the end of this conversation."

Immigration advocates, meanwhile, said the vote's outcome reflects the city's evolving identity.

"Every time this comes up, Nashville voters make clear that they want a city that welcomes everyone, regardless of what language they speak at home," Gonzalez said. "That was true in 2009, and it's true today."

The Metro Council has not indicated whether it will revisit the issue in future legislative sessions.

*This article reflects information available at the time of publication and may be updated as more details emerge.*
